## Direct Performance and Cost Evidence for Sodium-Ion Batteries

Sodium-ion battery technology is approaching the energy density performance of commercial lithium-ion batteries and is projected to deliver lower prices compared to lithium-ion systems as academic and start-up developments progress\. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.04963)

The theoretical cell parameters for average positive electrodes in sodium-ion chemistry versus sodium metal are estimated around 3\.3 volts, a specific capacity of approximately 170 milliamp-hours per gram, and a theoretical gravimetric energy density of roughly 560 watt-hours per kilogram\. [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04391)

## Uncertainties and Technical Bottlenecks

The long-term lifespan and cyclability of sodium-ion batteries require substantial improvement, although recent developments in positive electrode materials indicate potential advantages over lithium-ion electrodes if scaled up successfully\. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.04963)

Assessing beyond-lithium battery chemistries accurately requires establishing end-of-life energy density, long-term degradation mechanisms, and interfacial stability under varied practical operating conditions\. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.04963)

## Distinction from Alternative Sodium Chemistries and Grid-Level Gaps

High theoretical energy density sodium-sulphur and sodium-oxygen batteries operate via conversion reactions rather than the insertion and de-insertion mechanisms used in conventional sodium-ion cells, and while investigated for grid-scale stationary storage, they face distinct technology readiness challenges\. [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04391)

The retrieved literature on grid-connected storage focuses on technologies such as lithium-ion, sodium-sulphur, vanadium redox flow, and lead-acid, leaving direct field validation and economic assessments of sodium-ion batteries in stationary electricity markets unaddressed\. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00486)
